title: 17. Award Talk: Impact of a western style diet on the function and metabolism of the gastrointestinal tract in a swine model.
content:
Abstract
In the past two decades, there has been evidence of a shift in dietary trends, evolving away from a traditional diet towards a total western diet (TWD) that can be characterized by high levels of saturated fats, sugars, and refined foods. With this, it is integral to understand the effects that diet may have on the physiology of the gastrointestinal tract, specifically the gut microbiome. Therefore, the objective of the study was to evaluate the effects of a total wester diet on the fecal microbiome, fecal VFA, cytokines, and gene expression using swine as a biomedical model. A total of 30 York Landrace x Duroc gilts were randomly assigned to one of two treatment groups: a total western style diet (n = 15), or a high protein diet (n = 15). Gilts were fed their respective diets for eight weeks, before a total of ten gilts were selected for harvest (Pro_Short, n = 5; Sug_Short, n = 5). The remaining twenty gilts were reassigned to one of four treatment groups: continuing on the western style diet (Sug_Long, n = 5), continuing on the high protein diet (Pro_Long, n = 5), crossing over from the high protein diet to the western style diet (PS, n = 5), or crossing over from the western style diet to the high protein diet (SP, n = 5). The gilts were allowed a two-week acclimation period before being fed their new respective diets for an additional eight weeks. Fecal samples from all gilts were collected at the beginning (d1), middle (d63), and end (d118) of the study. At harvest, blood samples and mucosal samples from the small intestine were collected from all gilts. VFA were evaluated using gas chromatography, and cytokines were evaluated using Milliplex Porcine Cytokine/Chemokine Magnetic 13Plex Bead Panel. RT-qPCR was used to evaluate the expression of gut barrier genes using the mucosal samples. Microbial DNA was extracted followed by amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA V4 region on the MiSeq. QIIME2 was used for bioinformatic analyses, and ANCOM-BC was run to assess differential abundance across time point and treatment group at the phylum level. When comparing the initial and final time points, all treatment groups had enriched abundance of Planctomycetota, with the exception of the Sug_Long treatment (q ≤ 5.95e-6). In the Sug_Long, PS, and SP groups, Firimcutes were depleted between the final to initial time periods (q ≤ 0.008), and Bacteroidota was depleted during this time for the Sug_Long group (q = 0.008). Spirochaetoa was enriched in the Sug_Long and SP groups when comparing the middle to initial time periods (q ≤ 9.27e-7). Elusimicrobiota was also enriched in the Sug_Long group from the middle to initial periods (q = 1.83e-4), and in the final to initial periods for the PS group (q = 0.047). This indicates that a TWD can shift the composition of the microbiome at the phyla level over both short- and long-term periods of time. A principal component analysis was done to identify patterns among VFA, gene expression, cytokine, and microbiome metrics. The cytokine data contributed most to the factor scores, while gene expression contributed the least. VFA and microbiome metrics had average contribution to the factor scores. The TWD, specifically in long-term applications, may have lasting impacts on the gut microbiota that serve critical functions in the immune system, nutrient metabolism, and overall health of the animal.
